Measuring Kaplan–Meier Overestimation Under Competing Risks: Event Ordering, Quantification, and Exact Inference

Ferran Espuny-Pujol Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: University of Reading, UK Email: f.espuny-pujol@reading.ac.uk
November 11, 2026
Abstract

Competing risks arise when individuals may experience multiple mutually exclusive event types. Competing events are frequently treated as censoring and analysed using Kaplan–Meier (KM) methods, which overestimate real-world event risks. While the existence of KM overestimation is well known, its determinants, magnitude, and inferential properties remain poorly characterised.

We develop a nonparametric framework that treats competing risks overestimation as a statistical quantity in its own right. We show that competing event frequency alone is insufficient to characterise KM overestimation and develop an event ordering theory describing how temporal event allocation influences overestimation. Based on these results, we derive a closed-form Total Overestimation Diagnostic (TOD) that quantifies total KM overestimation directly from routine survival analysis output. We establish exact error equivalence results for both cause-specific and total overestimation. In particular, Product Limit Error Equivalence shows that inference for TOD reduces exactly to ordinary overall survival estimation.

Simulation experiments validate the theoretical results and show that independent censoring primarily affects precision rather than overestimation magnitude. Across six benchmark competing risks datasets, cause-specific overestimation is characterised by both total overestimation and temporal event allocation. These results provide a practical framework for assessing competing risks relevance and determining when cumulative incidence methods should be preferred to naïve KM risks.

The proposed framework transforms competing risks overestimation from a qualitative warning into a measurable quantity that can be routinely quantified, interpreted, and incorporated into reporting practice.

1 Introduction

Competing risks occur when individuals may experience multiple mutually exclusive event types, such that the occurrence of one event prevents the occurrence of the others [23, 12, 8]. Examples occur frequently in clinical and epidemiological research, including relapse versus non-relapse mortality following haematopoietic stem cell transplantation [9], progression to plasma cell myeloma versus death without prior progression in studies of monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) [17, 16], and numerous applications in oncology, cardiology, and ageing research [6, 8, 15]. In these settings, investigators are often interested in probabilities of clinically observable events, such as relapse within five years, disease progression before death, or death from a specific cause. These quantities are naturally described by cumulative incidence functions [21]. Their corresponding nonparametric estimator is the Aalen–Johansen (AJ) estimator [1, 11].

Competing risks are frequently ignored in routine practice. Reviews document frequent use of Kaplan–Meier (KM) methods in settings where cumulative incidence is the quantity of interest [5, 15]. The usual approach treats competing events as censoring and estimates event probabilities via the complement of the KM estimator. When competing events are treated as censoring, 1−S^KM,k​(t)1-\hat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t) does not estimate the cumulative incidence of event type kk. Instead, it estimates a net probability corresponding to a hypothetical setting in which competing events do not occur [21, 22]. As a result, KM estimation generally overstates event probabilities. For example, when estimating relapse following transplantation, deaths without relapse preclude subsequent relapse. Treating such deaths as censoring therefore evaluates the relapse risk that would have been observed had those deaths not occurred [9].

Although KM overestimation under competing risks is well recognised, its underlying structure remains poorly understood. The methodological literature provides extensive guidance on the analysis and interpretation of competing risks [21, 9, 4, 5]. Relatively little attention has been devoted to understanding the magnitude, determinants, and practical consequences of KM overestimation. In particular, the role of event ordering remains poorly understood. Direct comparison of KM and AJ estimates can reveal the presence of overestimation, but does not explain why overestimation occurs, what governs its magnitude, how it accumulates over time, or how uncertainty should be quantified. Competing event frequency is an obvious determinant of overestimation. However, datasets with similar competing event frequencies may exhibit markedly different levels of KM overestimation. This suggests that competing event frequency alone is insufficient for assessing competing risks relevance and raises more general questions regarding the mechanisms and practical consequences of KM overestimation.

The central idea of this paper is that KM overestimation under competing risks admits a formal theoretical characterisation through event ordering, quantification, and exact inference. We further show that this characterisation provides a principled basis for assessing competing risks relevance. Rather than viewing KM overestimation as a well recognised consequence of competing risks, we treat it as a measurable quantity that can be quantified, interpreted, subjected to formal inference, and incorporated into routine reporting. By characterising both the magnitude of overestimation and the mechanisms by which it arises, we develop a unified framework for understanding KM overestimation and assessing the practical relevance of competing risks.

The proposed framework has four complementary components. First, we develop an event ordering theory that characterises how temporal event allocation influences KM overestimation, including attainable bounds, local accumulation mechanisms, and extremal ordering configurations. Second, we introduce two complementary measures related to KM overestimation. The Total Overestimation Diagnostic (TOD) quantifies total KM overestimation, whereas the Order Index (OI) characterises temporal event allocation, which we show is a fundamental determinant of cause-specific KM overestimation. Third, we derive exact inferential results for both cause-specific and total overestimation, culminating in the Product Limit Error Equivalence theorem, which links inference for KM overestimation directly to standard KM survival inference.

Finally, we demonstrate how the proposed theory, measures, and inferential results can be used to assess competing risks relevance. Our results show that competing event frequency alone is insufficient. Rather, competing risks relevance depends on both the magnitude of total KM overestimation and the temporal allocation of event types.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section 2 introduces the competing risks framework and KM overestimation. Sections 3–5 develop the event ordering theory, cause-specific inference, TOD, and Product Limit Error Equivalence. Section 6 presents the empirical evaluation and Section 7 develops a practical interpretation framework to assess competing risks relevance in applied settings. Section 8 concludes with a discussion of implications, limitations, reporting recommendations, and future directions.

2 Competing Risks and KM Overestimation

2.1 Competing Risks Framework

Consider a competing risks setting with K≥2K\geq 2 mutually exclusive event types. Let TT denote the time to the first event and J∈{1,…,K}J\in\{1,\ldots,K\} its event type. Let CC denote the right censoring time. The observed data are X=min⁡(T,C)X=\min(T,C) and E=JE=J if T≤CT\leq C, with E=0E=0 otherwise [12, 8, 22]. The cause-specific cumulative incidence function plays a fundamental role in competing risks analysis and represents the real-world probability that an event of type kk has occurred by time tt in the presence of competing events. Formally,

Fk(t)=P(T≤t,J=k)=∫0tS(u−)λk(u)du,k=1,…,K,F_{k}(t)=\operatorname{P}(T\leq t,J=k)=\int_{0}^{t}S(u^{-})\lambda_{k}(u)\,du,\qquad k=1,\ldots,K, (1)

where S⁡(u−)=P⁡(T≥u)S(u^{-})=\operatorname{P}(T\geq u) denotes the overall event free survival function and λk​(u)\lambda_{k}(u) denotes the cause-specific hazard function for event type kk [1, 12, 8].

A key property of competing risks analysis is the overall risk decomposition identity, which expresses the probability of experiencing any event type by time tt as the sum of the cause-specific cumulative incidences [12, 22, 8]:

1−S⁡(t)=∑k=1KFk​(t).1-S(t)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}F_{k}(t). (2)

Let t1<t2<⋯<tmt_{1}<t_{2}<\cdots<t_{m} denote the ordered distinct event times across all causes. At each event time tit_{i}, r⁡(ti−)r(t_{i}^{-}) denotes the number of individuals remaining alive, event free, and under observation (risk set) immediately before tit_{i}, and dk​(ti)d_{k}(t_{i}) denotes the number of events of type kk occurring at tit_{i}, so that d⁡(ti)=∑k=1Kdk​(ti)d(t_{i})=\sum_{k=1}^{K}d_{k}(t_{i}) is the total number of events at tit_{i}.

The standard nonparametric estimator of the cumulative incidence function is the Aalen--Johansen (AJ) estimator11 1 Note that if an event occurs at tit_{i}, then necessarily d⁡(ti)≥1d(t_{i})\geq 1 and therefore r⁡(ti−)≥d⁡(ti)≥1r(t_{i}^{-})\geq d(t_{i})\geq 1. Hence, immediately before every observed event time the risk set is non-empty: r⁡(ti−)>0r(t_{i}^{-})>0, i=1,…,mi=1,\ldots,m. ,

F^kA​J​(t)=∑ti≤tS^P​L​(ti−1)​dk​(ti)r⁡(ti−),\widehat{F}_{k}^{AJ}(t)=\sum_{t_{i}\leq t}\widehat{S}_{PL}(t_{i-1})\frac{d_{k}(t_{i})}{r(t_{i}^{-})}, (3)

where

S^P​L​(t)=∏ti≤t(1−d⁡(ti)r⁡(ti−))\widehat{S}_{PL}(t)=\prod_{t_{i}\leq t}\left(1-\frac{d(t_{i})}{r(t_{i}^{-})}\right) (4)

is the overall product limit estimator of event free survival [1, 11, 8]. Equation (3) shows that cumulative incidence accumulates only through events of type kk, with each increment weighted by the overall event free survival probability immediately beforehand. Competing events therefore influence future cumulative incidence indirectly through their impact on event free survival [12, 22, 8]. Inference for cumulative incidence functions is commonly based on counting process methods and large sample theory [1, 12, 8].

In contrast, when competing events are treated as ordinary censoring, the cause-specific Kaplan–Meier (KM) estimator is [13]:

S^K​M,k​(t)=∏ti≤t(1−dk​(ti)r⁡(ti−)).\widehat{S}_{KM,k}(t)=\prod_{t_{i}\leq t}\left(1-\frac{d_{k}(t_{i})}{r(t_{i}^{-})}\right). (5)

Its complement, 1−S^K​M,k​(t)1-\widehat{S}_{KM,k}(t), is frequently interpreted and reported as an estimate of the probability of event type kk [5, 15].

Assumptions.

Unless stated otherwise, the results developed throughout this article assume a standard competing risks setting with independent right censoring [12, 3, 8]. Left truncation (delayed entry), interval censoring, and recurrent event processes are not considered.

2.2 Quantifying KM Overestimation

We begin by defining measures of KM overestimation for individual event types and for the competing risks setting as a whole.

Definition 1 (Empirical Cause-Specific Overestimation).

For event type kk, we define the empirical cause-specific KM overestimation at time tt as

B^k​(t)=(1−S^KM,k​(t))−F^kA​J​(t),\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}(t)=\left(1-\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t)\right)-\widehat{F}_{k}^{AJ}(t), (6)

where 1−S^KM,k​(t)1-\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t) denotes the cause-specific KM risk and F^kA​J​(t)\widehat{F}_{k}^{AJ}(t) denotes the corresponding AJ estimate of cumulative incidence.

Thus, B^k​(t)\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}(t) measures the extent to which the KM risk exceeds the corresponding AJ cumulative incidence estimate for event type kk.

In competing risks settings, cause-specific risks are interdependent because the occurrence of one event type removes the opportunity for the others to occur [2, 18]. Consequently, it is also informative to assess KM overestimation across the competing risks setting as a whole. Additionally, in some applications the competing risks system itself is the object of interest. For example, in a study about cause of mortality, the primary concern may be the overall impact of competing risks on estimated event probabilities, rather than overestimation for any particular event type. This motivates the introduction of a total measure of KM overestimation in addition to cause-specific overestimation measures.

Definition 2 (Empirical Total Overestimation).

We define the empirical total KM overestimation at time tt as the sum of cause-specific overestimations:

B^total​(t)=∑k=1KB^k​(t).\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{\mathrm{total}}(t)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}(t). (7)

Thus, B^total​(t)\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{\mathrm{total}}(t) measures the total discrepancy between cause-specific KM risks and their corresponding AJ cumulative incidence estimates across all competing event types. Section 5 derives an exact nonparametric representation of this aggregate quantity using only standard survival analysis estimators, yielding the Total Overestimation Diagnostic.

2.2.1 Decomposition of Empirical Cause-Specific KM Overestimation

The empirical cause-specific KM overestimation admits a useful decomposition obtained by combining the product limit representation of the KM estimator with the AJ estimator.

Lemma 1 (Overestimation Decomposition).

Under independent right censoring,

B^k​(t)=∑ti≤t[S^KM,k​(ti−1)−S^PL​(ti−1)]​dk​(ti)r⁡(ti−).\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}(t)=\sum_{t_{i}\leq t}\left[\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{i-1})-\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t_{i-1})\right]\frac{d_{k}(t_{i})}{r(t_{i}^{-})}. (8)
Derivation.

Equation (8) follows by combining the discrete-sum representation of the KM complement estimator [22],

1−S^KM,k​(t)=∑ti≤tS^KM,k​(ti−1)​dk​(ti)r⁡(ti−),1-\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t)=\sum_{t_{i}\leq t}\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{i-1})\frac{d_{k}(t_{i})}{r(t_{i}^{-})}, (9)

with the AJ estimator (3) and substituting both expressions into Equation (6). ∎

Equation (8) expresses empirical cause-specific KM overestimation as the interaction between a survival function gap generated by competing events and the subsequent occurrence of the event of interest. This representation suggests that the magnitude of KM overestimation may depend not only on competing event frequency but also on the temporal allocation of events. Section 3 investigates this possibility through the role of event ordering.

2.2.2 Accumulation of Empirical KM Overestimation

Equation (8) shows that empirical cause-specific KM overestimation accumulates through a sequence of non-negative local contributions. The following lemma formalises this accumulation property.

Lemma 2 (Non-Negativity and Monotonicity of Empirical KM Overestimation).

For each cause k∈{1,…,K}k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}, the empirical cause-specific overestimation function B^k​(t)\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}(t) is a non-negative, monotonically non-decreasing step function of follow-up time.

Consequently, the empirical total overestimation function B^total​(t)\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{\mathrm{total}}(t) is a non-negative, monotonically non-decreasing step function of follow-up time.

Proof.

From Equations (4) and (5), dk​(ti)≤d⁡(ti)d_{k}(t_{i})\leq d(t_{i}) at every event time implies that S^KM,k​(t)≥S^PL​(t)\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t)\geq\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t) for all t≥0t\geq 0. Equation (8) expresses B^k​(t)\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}(t) as a sum of non-negative terms, since S^KM,k​(ti−1)−S^PL​(ti−1)≥0\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{i-1})-\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t_{i-1})\geq 0, dk​(ti)≥0d_{k}(t_{i})\geq 0, and r⁡(ti−)>0r(t_{i}^{-})>0. Therefore, every increment is non-negative and B^k​(t)\widehat{B}_{k}(t) is a non-negative, monotonically non-decreasing step function of time. Finally, because B^total​(t)=∑k=1KB^k​(t)\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{\mathrm{total}}(t)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}(t) is a finite sum of non-negative, non-decreasing step functions, B^total​(t)\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{\mathrm{total}}(t) inherits these properties. ∎

3 The Role of Event Ordering

A common intuition in clinical biostatistics is that KM overestimation is driven primarily by competing event frequency, namely the proportion of individuals experiencing competing events [15, 5]. However, the decomposition in Equation (8) suggests that overestimation may also depend on the temporal allocation of events. This section investigates that possibility and shows that event ordering determines the attainable range of KM overestimation.

3.1 Illustrative Example: Reversing Event Ordering with Fixed Frequencies

To motivate the formal results that follow, Figure 1 compares two hypothetical cohorts adapted from Pepe and Mori [21]. Both cohorts contain N=100N=100 individuals, have identical follow-up duration (tmax=6t_{\max}=6 years), identical event frequencies (30 relapses and 40 competing deaths without relapse, followed by 30 observations subject to administrative censoring), and identical cause-specific cumulative incidences at six years: F1​(6)=0.30F_{1}(6)=0.30, F2​(6)=0.40F_{2}(6)=0.40. The only difference between the two cohorts is the temporal ordering of events.

Scenario A (Competing Events First). All competing deaths occur before any relapse. Consequently, the overall event free survival function S^PL​(t)\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t) declines before relapses begin, resulting in 1−S^KM,1​(6)=0.501-\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},1}(6)=0.50, and hence B^1​(6)=(1−S^KM,1​(6))−F1​(6)=0.20\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{1}(6)=\left(1-\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},1}(6)\right)-F_{1}(6)=0.20. Thus, KM overstates the 6-year relapse probability by 20%.

Scenario B (Relapses First). The event sequence is reversed while preserving event and censoring frequencies, follow-up duration, and cumulative incidences. All relapses occur before any competing death. Consequently, 1−S^KM,1​(6)=0.301-\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},1}(6)=0.30, and so B^1​(6)=0\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{1}(6)=0. Reversing the event sequence completely eliminates empirical cause-specific KM overestimation for event type 1 while preserving event and censoring frequencies, follow-up duration, and cumulative incidences [21]. Consequently, the observed difference in overestimation is attributable solely to event ordering.

This example demonstrates that event frequency alone does not determine KM overestimation and motivates the ordering results developed below.

Remark 1 (Mechanism of Event Ordering Overestimation).

By Equation (8), empirical cause-specific KM overestimation accumulates through the interaction between a survival function gap generated by competing events and the subsequent occurrence of events of interest. Early competing events enlarge this gap before future events of interest occur, whereas little gap develops when events of interest occur first. Event ordering therefore governs the magnitude of KM overestimation through the alignment between these two processes.

3.2 Ordering Bounds for Empirical Cause-Specific Overestimation

The preceding example and mechanism suggest that cause-specific KM overestimation may be bounded by extreme ordering configurations. We now characterise these bounds formally. For the ordering results below, event times are assumed to be distinct, d⁡(ti)≤1d(t_{i})\leq 1.

To formalize event ordering, consider a fixed observation skeleton consisting of fixed failure times, fixed censoring times, fixed numbers of events of type kk, and fixed numbers of competing events.

Let 𝒮F=(F1,…,Fm)∈{Ek,Ec}m\mathcal{S}_{F}=(F_{1},\ldots,F_{m})\in\{E_{k},E_{c}\}^{m} denote the ordered sequence of observed failure labels, where EkE_{k} denotes an observed event of type kk (E=kE=k) and EcE_{c} denotes an observed competing event (E∉{0,k}E\notin\{0,k\}).

Definition 3 (Failure Inversion Count).

The failure inversion count is defined as

I⁡(𝒮F)=∑1≤i<j≤m𝟏​(Fi=Ek,Fj=Ec).I(\mathcal{S}_{F})=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq m}\mathbf{1}\left(F_{i}=E_{k},\,F_{j}=E_{c}\right). (10)

Thus I⁡(𝒮F)I(\mathcal{S}_{F}) counts the number of instances in which an event of type kk occurs before a competing event. The unique zero inversion configuration 𝒮F∗=(Ec,…,Ec,Ek,…,Ek)\mathcal{S}_{F}^{\ast}=(E_{c},\ldots,E_{c},E_{k},\ldots,E_{k}) places all competing events before all events of type kk.

Definition 4 (Order Index).

The order index is defined as

O​I​(𝒮F)=1−I⁡(𝒮F)nk​nc,OI(\mathcal{S}_{F})=1-\frac{I(\mathcal{S}_{F})}{n_{k}n_{c}}\;, (11)

where I⁡(𝒮F)I(\mathcal{S}_{F}) is the inversion count, nkn_{k} is the number of events of interest, and ncn_{c} is the number of competing events.

OI values near 0 indicate that events of interest tend to occur before competing events, whereas values near 1 indicate that competing events tend to occur first. An OI near 0.50 corresponds to a balanced temporal allocation of event types.

3.2.1 Minimum Cause-Specific Overestimation Order

The event ordering that minimises empirical cause-specific KM overestimation corresponds to the following zero overestimation configuration.

Proposition 1 (Zero Cause-Specific Overestimation Boundary Condition).

For an event type kk with nk>0n_{k}>0,

B^k​(t)=0,∀t≥0,\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}(t)=0,\qquad\forall t\geq 0,

if and only if all competing events occur strictly after the final event of type kk:

𝒮F𝟘=(Ek,…,Ek,Ec,…,Ec).\mathcal{S}_{F}^{\mathbb{0}}=(E_{k},\ldots,E_{k},E_{c},\ldots,E_{c}).

Equivalently, O​I​(𝒮F𝟘)=0OI(\mathcal{S}_{F}^{\mathbb{0}})=0.

Proof.

(⇐)(\Leftarrow) If all competing events occur strictly after the final event of type kk, then S^KM,k​(ti−1)=S^PL​(ti−1)\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{i-1})=\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t_{i-1}) at every time tit_{i} of cause-specific event of type kk. Every summand in Equation (8) evaluates to zero, implying B^k​(t)=0\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}(t)=0 for all t≥0t\geq 0.

(⇒)(\Rightarrow) Suppose B^k​(t)=0\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}(t)=0 for all t≥0t\geq 0. By Equation (8), B^k​(t)\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}(t) is a sum of non-negative terms:

B^k​(t)=∑ti≤t[S^KM,k​(ti−1)−S^PL​(ti−1)]​dk​(ti)r⁡(ti−).\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}(t)=\sum_{t_{i}\leq t}\left[\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{i-1})-\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t_{i-1})\right]\frac{d_{k}(t_{i})}{r(t_{i}^{-})}.

For this sum to equal zero for all t≥0t\geq 0, every summand with dk​(ti)>0d_{k}(t_{i})>0 must be zero. Hence S^KM,k​(ti−1)=S^PL​(ti−1)\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{i-1})=\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t_{i-1}) at every time tit_{i} of cause-specific event of type kk. Suppose, for contradiction, that at least one competing event precedes an event of type kk. Let tct_{c} denote the time of the first competing event. At time tct_{c}, the competing event reduces overall event free survival to S^PL​(tc)=S^PL​(tc−)​(1−1r⁡(tc−))\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t_{c})=\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t_{c}^{-})\left(1-\frac{1}{r(t_{c}^{-})}\right) while leaving KM survival for events of type kk unchanged: S^KM,k​(tc)=S^KM,k​(tc−)\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{c})=\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{c}^{-}). Hence, S^KM,k​(tc)>S^PL​(tc)\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{c})>\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t_{c}).

Thereafter, censoring leaves both survival functions unchanged, events of type kk multiply both survival functions by the same positive factor, and competing events reduce only S^PL\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}. Consequently, the strict inequality is preserved until the next event of type kk occurs.

Let ti>tct_{i}>t_{c} denote the first subsequent event of type kk. At time tit_{i}, we have S^KM,k​(ti−1)>S^PL​(ti−1)\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{i-1})>\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t_{i-1}) and dk​(ti)>0d_{k}(t_{i})>0, yielding a strictly positive summand and implying B^k​(t)>0\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}(t)>0 for t≥tit\geq t_{i}, a contradiction. Therefore, no competing event can precede any event of type kk. Hence all competing events must occur strictly after the final event of type kk. ∎

3.2.2 Maximum Cause-Specific Overestimation Order

The zero overestimation boundary in Proposition 1 characterizes one extreme of the event ordering spectrum. We now determine the ordering configuration that maximizes cause-specific KM overestimation.

The next result characterises the pointwise effect of moving a competing event ahead of an adjacent event of type kk.

Lemma 3 (Transposition of Adjacent Failure Events).

Let 𝒮F\mathcal{S}_{F} contain two adjacent failure events (Fi,Fi+1)=(Ek,Ec)(F_{i},F_{i+1})=(E_{k},E_{c}) occurring at times ta<tbt_{a}<t_{b}, with c≥0c\geq 0 right censored observations between them. Let 𝒮F′\mathcal{S}^{\prime}_{F} denote the sequence obtained by interchanging the event labels, so that (Fi′,Fi+1′)=(Ec,Ek)(F_{i}^{\prime},F_{i+1}^{\prime})=(E_{c},E_{k}). Then the cause-kk Kaplan–Meier survival functions satisfy:

  1. 1.

    For t<tat<t_{a}, S^KM,k′​(t)=S^KM,k​(t)\widehat{S}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t)=\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t).

  2. 2.

    For ta≤t<tbt_{a}\leq t<t_{b}, S^KM,k′​(t)>S^KM,k​(t)\widehat{S}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t)>\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t).

  3. 3.

    At t=tbt=t_{b}, S^KM,k′​(tb)<S^KM,k​(tb)\widehat{S}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{b})<\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{b}).

  4. 4.

    For t≥tbt\geq t_{b}, S^KM,k′​(t)≤S^KM,k​(t)\widehat{S}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t)\leq\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t), with strict inequality unless both KM survival functions have reached zero.

Proof.

Let ra=r⁡(ta−)r_{a}=r(t_{a}^{-}) and rb=r⁡(tb−)=ra−1−cr_{b}=r(t_{b}^{-})=r_{a}-1-c.

Prior to tat_{a}, risk sets and event allocations are identical in both sequences, proving part 1.

On [ta,tb)[t_{a},t_{b}), sequence 𝒮F\mathcal{S}_{F} experiences the event EkE_{k} at tat_{a}, multiplying its cause-kk KM survival by 1−1/ra1-1/r_{a}. In 𝒮F′\mathcal{S}^{\prime}_{F}, the event at tat_{a} is competing and therefore does not alter cause-kk KM survival. Hence S^KM,k′​(t)\widehat{S}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t) = S^KM,k​(ta−)\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{a}^{-}) > S^KM,k​(ta−)​(1−1ra)\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{a}^{-})\left(1-\frac{1}{r_{a}}\right) = S^KM,k​(t)\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t), ta≤t<tbt_{a}\leq t<t_{b}, proving part 2.

At tbt_{b}, sequence 𝒮F′\mathcal{S}^{\prime}_{F} experiences the event EkE_{k} against the smaller risk set rb<rar_{b}<r_{a}. Therefore 1−1rb<1−1ra1-\frac{1}{r_{b}}<1-\frac{1}{r_{a}}, and consequently S^KM,k′​(tb)<S^KM,k​(tb)\widehat{S}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{b})<\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{b}), proving part 3.

After tbt_{b}, the two sequences have identical remaining event labels, failure times, censoring times, and risk sets. Subsequent cause-kk events therefore multiply both KM survival curves by the same non-negative factors, while censoring and competing events leave them unchanged. Hence S^KM,k′​(t)≤S^KM,k​(t)\widehat{S}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t)\leq\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t), t≥tbt\geq t_{b}. The inequality remains strict unless a subsequent common KM factor reduces both curves to zero. ∎

By the preceding lemma, once the transposed pair has occurred, an adjacent swap that removes an inversion increases the corresponding cause-specific KM risk. The resulting increase in empirical cause-specific KM overestimation can be quantified explicitly. For a transposition (Ek,Ec)→(Ec,Ek)(E_{k},E_{c})\rightarrow(E_{c},E_{k}) at times ta<tbt_{a}<t_{b},

Δ​B^k​(tb+)=B^k​(ta−)​(1+c)+S^PL​(ta−)ra​rb,\Delta\widehat{B}_{k}(t_{b}^{+})=\frac{\widehat{B}_{k}(t_{a}^{-})(1+c)+\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t_{a}^{-})}{r_{a}r_{b}}, (12)

where ra=r⁡(ta−)r_{a}=r(t_{a}^{-}) and rb=r⁡(tb−)=ra−1−cr_{b}=r(t_{b}^{-})=r_{a}-1-c. The increment is strictly positive and increases with previously accumulated overestimation, intervening censoring, and remaining event free survival. A derivation is provided in Appendix A.1.

The following theorem and corollary characterise the global optimum results arising from Lemma 3.

Theorem 1 (Global Maximum Ordering of Horizon Cause-Specific KM Risk).

For any fixed observation skeleton, fixed censoring schedule, fixed number of events of type kk, and fixed number of competing events, the zero inversion block allocation

𝒮F∗=(Ec,…,Ec,Ek,…,Ek)\mathcal{S}_{F}^{\ast}=(E_{c},\ldots,E_{c},E_{k},\ldots,E_{k})

attains the global maximum of the naïve cause-specific KM risk at any study horizon tmax≥tmt_{\max}\geq t_{m}: 1−S^KM,k​(tmax)1-\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{\max}). If r⁡(ti−)>1r(t_{i}^{-})>1 at every failure time in the fixed observation skeleton, then this maximising allocation is unique.

Proof.

The result follows by successively removing adjacent inversions. Each transposition cannot decrease cause-specific KM risk at the study horizon, and the process terminates at the zero inversion block allocation 𝒮F∗\mathcal{S}_{F}^{\ast}.

If I⁡(𝒮F)>0I(\mathcal{S}_{F})>0, the sequence contains at least one adjacent inversion (Ek,Ec)(E_{k},E_{c}). By Lemma 3, swapping this pair cannot decrease the cause-specific KM risk once both failures in the transposed pair have occurred, and therefore cannot decrease the risk at any study horizon tmax≥tmt_{\max}\geq t_{m}. The swap also reduces the inversion count by one. Repeated application of adjacent swaps that remove inversions generates a finite sequence

𝒮F(0)⟶𝒮F(1)⟶⋯⟶𝒮F∗,\mathcal{S}_{F}^{(0)}\longrightarrow\mathcal{S}_{F}^{(1)}\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow\mathcal{S}_{F}^{\ast},

terminating at the zero inversion block allocation. Because no swap decreases the horizon KM risk, 𝒮F∗\mathcal{S}_{F}^{\ast} attains the global maximum.

If r⁡(ti−)>1r(t_{i}^{-})>1 at every failure time, all cause-specific KM factors remain strictly positive. By Lemma 3, each adjacent swap that removes an inversion then produces a strict increase in horizon KM risk. Consequently, any sequence with I⁡(𝒮F)>0I(\mathcal{S}_{F})>0 has strictly smaller horizon KM risk than 𝒮F∗\mathcal{S}_{F}^{\ast}, proving uniqueness. ∎

Corollary 1 (Maximum Cause-Specific Overestimation Boundary Condition).

Let Bk​(tmax)=[1−S^KM,k​(tmax)]−Fk​(tmax)B_{k}(t_{\max})=\left[1-\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{\max})\right]-F_{k}(t_{\max}). For fixed Fk​(tmax)F_{k}(t_{\max}), theoretical horizon overestimation is globally maximised by the zero inversion block allocation 𝒮F∗\mathcal{S}_{F}^{\ast}.

If r⁡(ti−)>1r(t_{i}^{-})>1 at every failure time, this maximum is attained if and only if 𝒮F=𝒮F∗\mathcal{S}_{F}=\mathcal{S}_{F}^{\ast}.

Equivalently, O​I​(𝒮F∗)=1OI(\mathcal{S}_{F}^{\ast})=1.

Proof.

Since Fk​(tmax)F_{k}(t_{\max}) is fixed across all event permutations, maximizing Bk​(tmax)B_{k}(t_{\max}) is equivalent to maximizing 1−S^KM,k​(tmax)1-\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{\max}). Both results follow directly from Theorem 1. ∎

This section showed that event ordering is not merely associated with cause-specific KM overestimation but determines its attainable range at the study horizon under fixed event frequencies and censoring patterns.

The next section investigates the statistical properties of the empirical cause-specific KM overestimation estimator.

4 Exact Inference for Empirical Cause-Specific Overestimation

We now turn our attention to statistical inference. A natural question is whether empirical cause-specific KM overestimation requires its own inferential machinery or whether inference can be obtained from existing competing risks methodology.

4.1 AJ Error Equivalence

Recall the empirical cause-specific overestimation estimator defined by Equation (6), B^k​(t)=(1−S^KM,k​(t))−F^kAJ​(t)\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}(t)=\left(1-\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t)\right)-\widehat{F}_{k}^{\mathrm{AJ}}(t), and define the corresponding target quantity

Bk⁡(t)=(1−S^KM,k​(t))−Fk​(t),\operatorname{B}_{k}(t)=\left(1-\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t)\right)-F_{k}(t), (13)

where Fk​(t)F_{k}(t) denotes the true cause-specific cumulative incidence function. The quantity Bk⁡(t)\operatorname{B}_{k}(t) represents the true cause-specific KM overestimation at time tt.

Theorem 2 (AJ Error Equivalence).

For any event type k∈{1,…,K}k\in\{1,\dots,K\} and any follow-up time t≥0t\geq 0,

B^k​(t)−Bk⁡(t)=Fk​(t)−F^kAJ​(t).\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}(t)-\operatorname{B}_{k}(t)=F_{k}(t)-\widehat{F}_{k}^{\mathrm{AJ}}(t). (14)
Proof.

Subtracting Equation (13) from Equation (6) gives

B^k​(t)−Bk⁡(t)\displaystyle\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}(t)-\operatorname{B}_{k}(t) =[(1−S^KM,k​(t))−F^kAJ​(t)]−[(1−S^KM,k​(t))−Fk​(t)]\displaystyle=\Big[\left(1-\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t)\right)-\widehat{F}_{k}^{\mathrm{AJ}}(t)\Big]-\Big[\left(1-\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t)\right)-F_{k}(t)\Big]
=Fk​(t)−F^kAJ​(t),\displaystyle=F_{k}(t)-\widehat{F}_{k}^{\mathrm{AJ}}(t),

which proves Equation (14). ∎

4.2 Inferential Consequences for Cause-Specific Overestimation

The AJ Error Equivalence theorem immediately yields the following consistency and exact variance inheritance results.

Corollary 2 (Cause-Specific Overestimation Consistency Inheritance).

Under independent right censoring and a non-vanishing risk set, the empirical cause-specific overestimation estimator B^k\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k} is uniformly consistent for Bk\operatorname{B}_{k}:

‖B^k−Bk‖∞→P0.\|\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}-\operatorname{B}_{k}\|_{\infty}\xrightarrow{\operatorname{P}}0. (15)
Proof.

Under independent right censoring and a non-vanishing risk set, the AJ estimator is uniformly consistent, ‖Fk−F^kA​J‖∞→P0\|F_{k}-\widehat{F}_{k}^{AJ}\|_{\infty}\xrightarrow{\operatorname{P}}0 [1, 12, 8]. By Theorem 2, ‖B^k−Bk‖∞=‖Fk−F^kA​J‖∞→P0\|\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}-\operatorname{B}_{k}\|_{\infty}=\|F_{k}-\widehat{F}_{k}^{AJ}\|_{\infty}\xrightarrow{\operatorname{P}}0, which gives the result. ∎

Corollary 3 (Cause-Specific Overestimation Variance Inheritance).

For any event type k∈{1,…,K}k\in\{1,\dots,K\} and follow-up time t≥0t\geq 0,

Var⁡(B^k​(t)−Bk⁡(t))=Var⁡(F^kAJ​(t)).\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}(t)-\operatorname{B}_{k}(t)\right)=\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\widehat{F}_{k}^{\mathrm{AJ}}(t)\right). (16)
Proof.

Taking variances on both sides of Equation (14) gives Var⁡(B^k​(t)−Bk⁡(t))=Var⁡(Fk​(t)−F^kAJ​(t))\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}(t)-\operatorname{B}_{k}(t)\right)=\operatorname{Var}\!\left(F_{k}(t)-\widehat{F}_{k}^{\mathrm{AJ}}(t)\right).

Since Fk​(t)F_{k}(t) is non-random, Var⁡(Fk​(t)−F^kAJ​(t))=Var⁡(F^kAJ​(t))\operatorname{Var}\!\left(F_{k}(t)-\widehat{F}_{k}^{\mathrm{AJ}}(t)\right)=\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\widehat{F}_{k}^{\mathrm{AJ}}(t)\right), which proves Equation (16). ∎

Theorem 2 and Corollaries 2–3 show that empirical cause-specific KM overestimation inherits the inferential framework of the AJ estimator. As a result, standard AJ confidence intervals, variance estimators, and large sample results apply directly to cause-specific KM overestimation without modification or additional asymptotic theory. Inference reduces directly to inference for the corresponding AJ estimator.

5 Exact Diagnostic for Empirical Total KM Overestimation

We now extend the previous cause-specific framework to the competing risks setting as a whole. This section addresses three related questions.

How can total KM overestimation be quantified?
How can uncertainty in total KM overestimation be quantified?
Is total KM overestimation an unavoidable feature of competing risks settings?

The resulting Total Overestimation Diagnostic (TOD) quantifies empirical total KM overestimation across all competing event types using only standard nonparametric survival estimators. Figure 2 illustrates TOD in the MGUS cohort. Full details on this empirical evaluation are provided in Section 6.2.

5.1 Exact Quantification of Total Overestimation

The first question is straightforward: How large is total KM overestimation?

The following theorem provides a closed-form quantification of empirical total KM overestimation through the Total Overestimation Diagnostic (TOD).

Theorem 3 (Closed-Form Total Overestimation Diagnostic).

Under independent right censoring and a non-vanishing risk set, the empirical total KM overestimation B^total​(t)\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{\mathrm{total}}(t) can be calculated as

T​O​D​(t)=S^PL​(t)−∑k=1KS^KM,k​(t)+(K−1).\boxed{TOD(t)=\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t)-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t)+(K-1).} (17)

Theorem 3 provides an exact measure of total KM overestimation using only standard overall product limit and cause-specific KM estimators. In particular, total KM overestimation can be quantified directly from routine survival analysis output without requiring cumulative incidence calculations.

Proof.

Substituting Equation (6) into B^total​(t)=∑k=1KB^k​(t)\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{\mathrm{total}}(t)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}(t) and using the risk decomposition identity for the AJ estimator [12, 8], ∑k=1KF^kAJ​(t)=1−S^PL​(t)\sum_{k=1}^{K}\widehat{F}_{k}^{\mathrm{AJ}}(t)=1-\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t), yields Equation (17). ∎

Remark 2 (TOD for Two Competing Risks).

For the common case of two competing event types (K=2K=2), Equation (17) for quantifying B^total​(t)\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{\mathrm{total}}(t) simplifies to

T​O​D​(t)=S^PL​(t)−S^KM,1​(t)−S^KM,2​(t)+1.TOD(t)=\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t)-\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},1}(t)-\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},2}(t)+1.

This representation allows total KM overestimation to be calculated directly from three standard survival curves.

5.2 Exact Inference for Total Overestimation

The second question concerns statistical inference: How can uncertainty in total overestimation be quantified?

The following theorem is the key inferential result of this paper. It determines an exact, finite sample error equivalence identity between the total overestimation diagnostic and the overall product limit estimator.

5.2.1 Product Limit Error Equivalence

The Total Overestimation Diagnostic (TOD) introduced above possesses a remarkable inferential property. Define the target total overestimation quantity as

Btotal⁡(t)=∑k=1KBk⁡(t)​=(13,2)​(1−S⁡(t))−∑k=1KS^KM,k​(t)+(K−1),\operatorname{B}_{\mathrm{total}}(t)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\operatorname{B}_{k}(t)\overset{(\ref{eq:true_bias_def},\ref{eq:risk_decomposition})}{=}\left(1-S(t)\right)-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t)+(K-1), (18)

where S⁡(t)=P⁡(T>t)S(t)=\operatorname{P}(T>t) denotes the true overall event free survival function. The quantity Btotal⁡(t)\operatorname{B}_{\mathrm{total}}(t) represents the total KM overestimation that would be observed if the true overall survival function S⁡(t)S(t) were known.

Theorem 4 (Product Limit Error Equivalence).

For any follow-up time t≥0t\geq 0,

B^total​(t)−Btotal⁡(t)=S^PL​(t)−S⁡(t).\boxed{\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{\mathrm{total}}(t)-\operatorname{B}_{\mathrm{total}}(t)=\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t)-S(t).} (19)
Proof.

Aggregating the cause-specific error-equivalence identity of Theorem 2 over all event types k=1,…,Kk=1,\dots,K gives

B^total​(t)−Btotal⁡(t)=∑k=1KFk​(t)−∑k=1KF^kAJ​(t).\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{\mathrm{total}}(t)-\operatorname{B}_{\mathrm{total}}(t)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}F_{k}(t)-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\widehat{F}_{k}^{\mathrm{AJ}}(t).

Using the theoretical and empirical risk decomposition identities [12, 8], ∑k=1KFk​(t)​=(2)​1−S⁡(t)\sum_{k=1}^{K}F_{k}(t)\overset{\eqref{eq:risk_decomposition}}{=}1-S(t) and ∑k=1KF^kAJ​(t)=1−S^PL​(t)\sum_{k=1}^{K}\widehat{F}_{k}^{\mathrm{AJ}}(t)=1-\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t), gives Equation (19). ∎

Theorem 4 reveals a complete simplification of the total overestimation inferential problem. Inference for total KM overestimation is not merely asymptotically equivalent to inference for overall survival; the two error processes are algebraically identical for every sample and every follow-up time.

5.2.2 Inferential Consequences for the Total Overestimation Diagnostic

The Product Limit Error Equivalence theorem immediately yields consistency and exact variance inheritance for the total overestimation diagnostic.

Corollary 4 (Total Overestimation Consistency Inheritance).

Under independent right censoring and a non-vanishing risk set, the empirical total overestimation estimator B^total\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{\mathrm{total}} is uniformly consistent for Btotal\operatorname{B}_{\mathrm{total}}:

‖B^total−Btotal‖∞→P0.\|\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{\mathrm{total}}-\operatorname{B}_{\mathrm{total}}\|_{\infty}\xrightarrow{\operatorname{P}}0. (20)
Proof.

Under independent right censoring (assumption of Section 2.1), the product limit estimator for overall event free survival is uniformly consistent [1, 8], and so ‖S^PL−S‖∞→P0\|\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}-S\|_{\infty}\xrightarrow{\operatorname{P}}0.

Applying Theorem 4, we get: ‖B^total−Btotal‖∞=‖S^PL−S‖∞→P0\|\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{\mathrm{total}}-\operatorname{B}_{\mathrm{total}}\|_{\infty}=\|\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}-S\|_{\infty}\xrightarrow{\operatorname{P}}0. ∎

Corollary 5 (Total Overestimation Variance Inheritance).

For any follow-up time t≥0t\geq 0,

Var⁡(B^total​(t)−Btotal⁡(t))=Var⁡(S^PL​(t)).\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{\mathrm{total}}(t)-\operatorname{B}_{\mathrm{total}}(t)\right)=\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t)\right). (21)
Proof.

Taking variances on both sides of Equation (19) gives Var⁡(B^total​(t)−Btotal⁡(t))=Var⁡(S^PL​(t)−S⁡(t))\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{\mathrm{total}}(t)-\operatorname{B}_{\mathrm{total}}(t)\right)=\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t)-S(t)\right).

Since S⁡(t)S(t) is non-random, the previous equality can be simplified as Equation (21). ∎

Consequently, all standard product limit inferential procedures [12, 8] apply directly to TOD.

5.3 Structural Properties of Total Overestimation

A fundamental question is whether total overestimation can ever be absent. If total overestimation is merely a possible consequence of competing risks, its practical importance may depend on the specific dataset under study. The following result establishes a stronger conclusion.

Theorem 5 (Structural Positivity of Total Overestimation at Horizon).

Consider a competing risks setting with K≥2K\geq 2 event types. Let tmaxt_{\max} denote the study horizon, with tmax≥tmt_{\max}\geq t_{m}, where tmt_{m} is the final observed failure time. If at least two distinct event types occur during follow-up, then the Total Overestimation Diagnostic is strictly positive at end of follow-up:

B^total​(tmax)>0.\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{\mathrm{total}}(t_{\max})>0. (22)
Proof.

Without loss of generality, assume that the first occurring failure event belongs to event type 1 and occurs at time t1t_{1}, and let tc>t1t_{c}>t_{1} denote the first occurrence of a different realised event type, labelled event type 2.

At time t1t_{1}, the overall product limit survival estimator decreases, S^PL​(t1)=1−1r⁡(t1−)<1\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t_{1})=1-\frac{1}{r(t_{1}^{-})}<1, whereas the event type 2 Kaplan–Meier survival estimator remains unchanged, S^KM,2​(t1)=1\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},2}(t_{1})=1. Consequently, S^KM,2​(t1)−S^PL​(t1)=1r⁡(t1−)>0\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},2}(t_{1})-\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t_{1})=\frac{1}{r(t_{1}^{-})}>0.

At time tc−t_{c}^{-}, this survival gap remains strictly positive. Since the event at time tct_{c} is of type 2, Equation (8) implies that the corresponding increment in B^2​(tc)\widehat{B}_{2}(t_{c}) is strictly positive: B^2​(tc)>0\widehat{B}_{2}(t_{c})>0.

By Lemma 2, B^2​(tmax)≥B^2​(tc)>0\widehat{B}_{2}(t_{\max})\geq\widehat{B}_{2}(t_{c})>0.

Moreover, empirical overestimation is non-negative for every cause, B^k​(tmax)≥0\widehat{B}_{k}(t_{\max})\geq 0, k=1,…,Kk=1,\dots,K.

Finally, B^total​(tmax)=∑k=1KB^k​(tmax)≥B^2​(tmax)≥B^2​(tc)>0.\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{\mathrm{total}}(t_{\max})=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\widehat{B}_{k}(t_{\max})\geq\widehat{B}_{2}(t_{\max})\geq\widehat{B}_{2}(t_{c})>0. ∎

Remark 3 (Total Overestimation is Structurally Unavoidable).

In any competing risks dataset containing at least two distinct realised event types, the Total Overestimation Diagnostic cannot vanish at study horizon. Consequently, total Kaplan–Meier overestimation is an unavoidable structural feature of the observed competing risks setting whenever at least two event types occur.

The practical significance of Section 5 is threefold. TOD provides an exact diagnostic for total KM overestimation using only standard survival analysis estimators. Product Limit Error Equivalence reduces uncertainty quantification for TOD to ordinary overall survival estimation. Structural positivity establishes that total KM overestimation is unavoidable whenever multiple event types are realised. Consequently, total overestimation is not a phenomenon that must first be detected; it is always present and it must be quantified and reported.

Together, event ordering theory, TOD, Product Limit Error Equivalence, and Structural Positivity imply that KM overestimation is an unavoidable, measurable, inferable, and reportable feature of competing risks settings.

The next section evaluates these theoretical results using benchmark datasets and simulation studies before turning to their implications for assessing competing risks relevance.

6 Empirical Evaluation

6.1 Benchmark Competing Risk Datasets
(Frequency alone is insufficient)

To evaluate the empirical behaviour of the proposed framework, we analysed six benchmark datasets widely used in survival and competing risks research. The datasets span plasma cell disorders, hepatology, oncology, transplantation, and acute leukaemia.

The benchmark panel includes the MGUS cohort, where progression to plasma cell malignancy competes with death without prior progression [17, 16]; the PBC and UDCA cohorts, where death competes with liver transplantation [25, 20]; the MELANOMA cohort, where melanoma-specific mortality competes with death from other causes [3]; the TRANSPLANT cohort, where liver transplantation competes with waiting list mortality [14]; and the MYELOID cohort, where relapse competes with death before relapse [19].

These datasets were chosen because they are widely used benchmark examples in the survival, multi-state and competing risks literature. For comparability, each dataset was administratively censored at a clinically meaningful fixed horizon, and event definitions were harmonised to define a single event of interest and a single competing event.

Table 1 demonstrates considerable heterogeneity in KM overestimation across these widely used benchmark datasets. Cause-specific KM overestimation ranged from 0.4% in the UDCA cohort to 14.6% in MGUS, while TOD ranged from 0.6% to 28.7%.

These results indicate that competing event frequency alone is insufficient to characterise the magnitude of overestimation. For example, the MYELOID and UDCA cohorts exhibited similar competing event frequencies (40.2% and 38.9%, respectively), yet differed almost twenty fold in observed KM overestimation (7.7% versus 0.4%).

6.2 Empirical Application: MGUS Cohort
(TOD is measurable and reportable)

To evaluate the empirical behaviour of the proposed framework, we analysed the classical Monoclonal Gammopathy of Undetermined Significance (MGUS) cohort, a widely used competing risks benchmark dataset describing progression to plasma cell malignancy or death of 241 patients [17, 16, 8]. For comparability, follow-up was administratively censored at 25 years. At this horizon, 58 patients (24.1%) had progressed to plasma cell malignancy, 145 (60.2%) had died before progression, and 38 (15.8%) remained event free.

Figure 2 presents both the conventional KM versus AJ comparison and the corresponding Total Overestimation Diagnostic. Across the observed 25 year follow-up period, mean progression KM overestimation was approximately 4.8 percentage points, mean competing mortality KM overestimation was approximately 3.5 percentage points, and mean total KM overestimation was approximately 8.3 percentage points. These means provide descriptive summaries across follow-up. At the prespecified 25-year horizon, TOD was 0.287, indicating that the sum of the cause-specific KM risks exceeded the corresponding cumulative incidences by 28.7 percentage points (95% CI, 0.247–0.341).

To verify the closed-form identity numerically, we defined the diagnostic residual R⁡(t)=B^total​(t)−∑k=1KB^k​(t)R(t)=\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{\mathrm{total}}(t)-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}(t). As predicted by Theorem 3, TOD recovered the observed total overestimation across the entire follow-up period, to numerical precision.

Confidence intervals for TOD were obtained directly from standard product limit confidence limits through Product Limit Error Equivalence. The resulting confidence bands behaved as predicted, confirming that uncertainty quantification for total overestimation requires no competing risks specific inferential machinery.

The MGUS cohort illustrates how TOD converts that overestimation into a reportable quantity with formal statistical uncertainty. Together with Structural Positivity (Theorem 5), this shifts the practical question from whether total overestimation exists to how large it is. TOD thus provides a practical audit metric for KM overestimation in routine competing risks analyses.

6.3 Frequency, Ordering, and the Magnitude of KM Overestimation
(Ordering matters)

The event ordering theory developed in Section 3 predicts that the magnitude of KM overestimation depends not only on competing event frequency but also on the temporal ordering of competing events and events of interest. To investigate the practical implications of this result, we conducted a large scale simulation study spanning a broad range of competing risk settings. Simulated datasets were generated under varying competing event frequencies and ordering structures, using a fixed sample size of N=500 and approximately 20% independent right censoring. Complete simulation details are provided in Appendix B.1, while calibration and quality control diagnostics are reported in Appendix B.2.

Figure 3 summarises mean cause-specific KM overestimation for the event of interest (Panel A) and mean Total Overestimation Diagnostic (TOD; Panel B) under representative simulation settings. The vertical axis corresponds to the Order Index (OI) defined by Equation (11), with lower values indicating that events of interest tend to occur earlier than competing events and higher values indicating the opposite.

Several findings emerge. Most importantly, event ordering materially alters both cause-specific and total overestimation even when competing event frequency is held fixed. The influence of ordering becomes increasingly pronounced as competing event frequency increases. At low competing event frequencies, differences between ordering configurations are comparatively modest. At moderate and high competing event frequencies, however, markedly different levels of overestimation arise under identical competing event frequencies but different Order Index values.

Cause-specific and total overestimation also exhibit distinct behaviour. Configurations producing the largest overestimation for the event of interest do not necessarily produce the largest TOD values. This observation suggests that mechanisms governing extremal cause-specific and total overestimation may differ, highlighting the distinction between cause-specific and total measures of overestimation.

The simulations provide empirical support for the event ordering theory developed in Section 3. They further show that the practical importance of event ordering increases as competing event frequency increases, with markedly different levels of KM overestimation arising under identical competing event frequencies but different temporal event allocations. These results confirm that temporal event allocation is an independent determinant of both cause-specific and total KM overestimation.

6.4 Censoring Stress Test
(Product Limit Error Equivalence works)

The Product Limit Error Equivalence theorem predicts that independent censoring should primarily affect the precision of total overestimation estimation rather than the magnitude of total KM overestimation. To evaluate this prediction, we simulated five censoring settings ranging from complete follow-up to heavy random censoring. Figure 4 summarises the resulting distributions of total overestimation.

Across all censoring settings, total overestimation remained remarkably stable. At five years, mean total overestimation ranged from approximately 0.207 in the uncensored setting to 0.209 under the heaviest configuration (Appendix B.3). In contrast, estimator variability increased markedly with censoring intensity. The standard deviation of total overestimation increased from approximately 0.027 to 0.121, representing a 4.5-fold increase in variability.

These results demonstrate a clear separation between magnitude and precision. Independent censoring has little effect on underlying overestimation, but considerably reduces the precision with which that overestimation can be estimated. The observed behaviour is therefore consistent with the prediction of Product Limit Error Equivalence.

7 A Practical Interpretation Framework

Two practical questions remain unresolved. First, given that both event ordering and competing event frequency influence KM overestimation, how their effects can be quantified and their relative importance determined. Secondly, how competing risks relevance should be assessed in routine applications and, consequently, when cumulative incidence methods should be preferred to naïve KM risks.

7.1 Empirical Characterisation of Cause-Specific Overestimation

To address the first question, we investigated how cause-specific KM overestimation at horizon (end of follow-up) relates to total overestimation (TOD) at horizon, competing event frequency, and event ordering measured by Order Index (OI) across the simulation design from Section 6.3. To characterise this relationship, a sequence of increasingly complex models was fitted using the simulated datasets. Simulation performance was evaluated using adjusted R2R^{2} and external validation using the six benchmark datasets. Complete model results are reported in Appendix B.1. Table 2 summarises the principal findings.

The benchmark validation results suggest two particularly useful empirical relationships for characterising cause-specific overestimation:

B^k​(tmax)≃0.5​T​O​D,\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}(t_{\max})\simeq 0.5\,TOD, (23)
B^k​(tmax)≃(0.13+0.79​O​I)​T​O​D.\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}(t_{\max})\simeq\left(0.13+0.79\,OI\right)\,TOD\;. (24)

Several more complex models achieved higher adjusted R2R^{2} values on the simulated data. However, the TOD×\timesOI relationship generalised most effectively to the benchmark datasets (MAE=0.007), outperforming models based on competing event frequency alone, OI alone, TOD alone, and more complex model specifications. These results suggest that the combined information contained in TOD and OI captures the principal determinants of cause-specific overestimation, whereas competing event frequency provides comparatively little additional explanatory value.

Since the TOD×\timesOI relationship achieved the strongest external validation performance, it provides an empirical characterisation of the principal determinants of cause-specific overestimation. Specifically, Equation (24) can be rewritten as

B^k​(tmax)T​O​D​(tmax)≃0.13+0.79​O​I,\boxed{\frac{\widehat{\operatorname{B}}_{k}(t_{\max})}{TOD(t_{\max})}\simeq 0.13+0.79\,OI\;,} (25)

which quantifies how the share of total overestimation corresponding to the event of interest depends on OI.

Equation (23) suggests that, in the absence of additional information, cause-specific overestimation is approximately one half of total overestimation. Equation (25) refines this relationship through OI, providing a quantitative interpretation of how event ordering influences cause-specific overestimation.

This interpretation is closely related to the classical competing risks framework. Lower OI values imply that events of interest occur earlier and the risk set depletion due to competing events occurs later, reducing cause-specific KM overestimation. Conversely, higher OI values imply earlier risk set depletion so that cause-specific overestimation represents a larger share of total overestimation.

Finally, note that the relationships (23) and (25) generalised well to the benchmark datasets despite considerable variation in sample size and censoring frequency. This suggests that the relationships identified by the simulation study (n=500 and 20% of censoring) are not highly sensitive to the specific sample size and censoring configuration used during model development.

7.2 Implications for Assessing Competing Risks Relevance

We now return to the practical question motivating this work: how should competing risks relevance be assessed in routine applications and, consequently, when should cumulative incidence methods be preferred to naive KM risks?

We suggest a simple assessment workflow. First, compute TOD and its confidence interval. If TOD is sufficiently small, competing risks overestimation is unlikely to have practical consequences. If TOD is not negligible, further analysis should depend on the scientific objective. If interest lies in the competing risks system as a whole, a non-negligible TOD reveals that competing risks are practically relevant. If interest centres on a particular event, cause-specific overestimation should be examined directly through KM–CIF comparisons for the event of interest. The choice of what constitutes a negligible TOD is application dependent and should reflect the maximum discrepancy investigators are willing to tolerate between KM and cumulative incidence estimates.

The rationale for beginning with TOD is straightforward. TOD quantifies total KM overestimation across the competing risks system, whereas cause-specific overestimation depends on the choice of event of interest. Since cause-specific overestimation cannot exceed total overestimation, a small TOD implies uniformly small cause-specific overestimation for all event types. Consequently, when TOD is judged negligible, competing risks are unlikely to materially affect any conclusions regardless of the endpoint under study.

The role of OI is interpretive rather than diagnostic. TOD and KM–CIF comparisons quantify the magnitude of overestimation, at total and cause-specific levels, whereas OI helps explain why the latter overestimation occurs. By quantifying temporal event allocation, OI summarises the risk set depletion mechanisms that drive cause-specific overestimation.

Together, TOD and OI provide a practical framework for assessing competing risks relevance. TOD quantifies the magnitude of total KM overestimation, whereas OI explains how temporal event allocation influences cause-specific overestimation for a particular event of interest. The results of this study therefore suggest that competing risks relevance depends on both the magnitude of total KM overestimation and the temporal allocation of event types, rather than on competing event frequency alone.

8 Discussion

This paper developed a framework for understanding competing risks overestimation. Rather than treating overestimation as a qualitative consequence of applying Kaplan–Meier methods in the presence of competing risks, the proposed framework allows overestimation to be explained, quantified, subjected to formal inference, and interpreted, thereby providing a practical basis for assessing the relevance of competing risks in routine analyses.

The first question addressed by the framework is: What determines KM overestimation? Previous discussions of competing risks overestimation have largely focused on its existence and on the role of competing event frequency [21, 22, 5]. By contrast, the present work showed that cause-specific overestimation possesses an explicit temporal structure arising from the interaction between competing events and events of interest. The ordering results identified attainable lower and upper overestimation boundaries, characterised the local accumulation mechanism, introduced the Order Index, and provided a complete ordering that maximises horizon cause-specific KM overestimation. These results establish event ordering as an independent determinant of overestimation magnitude.

The empirical analyses reinforced this interpretation. Benchmark datasets demonstrated considerable heterogeneity in overestimation despite similar competing event frequencies, while simulation experiments showed that ordering effects become increasingly pronounced as competing event frequency increases. These findings indicate that temporal event allocation is an important source of heterogeneity in the practical behaviour of KM overestimation. They also highlight an important distinction between cause-specific and total overestimation: configurations producing maximal cause-specific overestimation for one event type do not necessarily produce maximal total overestimation. Therefore, cause-specific and total overestimation perspectives should not be regarded as interchangeable.

The second question addressed by the framework is: How much overestimation exists? The Total Overestimation Diagnostic (TOD) converts competing risks overestimation into a directly measurable quantity that can be obtained from routine survival analysis output. Importantly, Structural Positivity showed that total KM overestimation is an unavoidable feature of realised competing risks settings. TOD therefore quantifies the magnitude of this unavoidable overestimation. The benchmark datasets demonstrated substantial heterogeneity in TOD, even among settings with similar competing event frequencies, reinforcing the distinction between competing event frequency and actual overestimation. By making total overestimation observable, TOD provides a practical audit metric and establishes a quantitative basis for assessing the relevance of competing risks in routine analyses.

The third question addressed by the framework is: How should uncertainty in competing risks overestimation be quantified? AJ Error Equivalence showed that inference for empirical cause-specific overestimation inherits directly from the Aalen–Johansen estimator. At the competing risks setting level, Product Limit Error Equivalence demonstrated that inference for TOD reduces exactly, rather than asymptotically, to ordinary overall survival estimation. Consequently, confidence intervals, standard errors, and uncertainty quantification for competing risks overestimation can be obtained using existing survival analysis methodology, without covariance modelling, bootstrap resampling, or inferential procedures specific to competing risks. This reduction in inferential complexity substantially lowers the practical barrier to uncertainty quantification for competing risks overestimation.

The framework concluded by addressing two practical questions: How can cause-specific overestimation be characterised? When are competing risks practically important?
In the absence of additional information, cause-specific overestimation is approximately one half of total overestimation on average. Incorporating event ordering substantially refines this relationship. TOD quantifies how much competing risks overestimation exists, whereas the Order Index (OI) provides an interpretation of the resulting cause-specific overestimation.
Together, TOD and OI provide a practical framework for assessing competing risks relevance. Since cause-specific overestimation cannot exceed total overestimation, small TOD values imply uniformly small cause-specific overestimation across all event types. Accordingly, we propose to first assess whether TOD is negligible. If TOD is sufficiently small, cause-specific overestimation must also be small for every event type, and competing risks are unlikely to materially affect substantive conclusions. If TOD is not negligible and the study interest lies on a particular event, cause-specific overestimation should be quantified directly through KM–CIF comparisons for that event. The role of OI is then interpretive rather than diagnostic. This part of the framework provides the practical counterpart to the event ordering theory developed in Section 3.

Several limitations should be acknowledged. The theoretical results were developed under a standard competing risks setting with independent right censoring and without delayed entry, interval censoring, recurrent event processes, or time dependent covariates. The ordering results describe structural properties of observed competing risks trajectories and should not be interpreted causally. Finally, although the theoretical contributions apply to an arbitrary number of event types, the empirical illustrations focused primarily on settings with two competing event types.

Future work may extend the framework beyond standard independent censoring. Particularly important directions include the development of covariate adjusted versions of TOD, extensions to multi-state and progressive disease processes, and characterisation of the event allocation that maximises total overestimation across an entire competing risks setting.

The proposed framework allows the relevance of competing risks to be assessed explicitly rather than merely inferred. By quantifying total overestimation (TOD), directly evaluating cause-specific overestimation when necessary, and using temporal allocation of events (OI) to interpret the resulting discrepancies, the practical relevance of competing risks can be evaluated directly from observed data. TOD provides the assessment; KM–CIF provides event-specific quantification; OI provides the interpretation. This provides a principled basis for determining when naïve KM risks remain reasonable approximations of real-world event probabilities and when cumulative incidence methods become necessary. In this sense, competing risks overestimation becomes not simply a methodological limitation of KM estimation, but a routinely measurable quantity that can inform analytic and reporting decisions.

Software and Reproducibility.

All empirical analyses were conducted using R version 4.4.1 [24]. Survival and competing risks estimation used the survival version 3.8.6 and cmprsk version 2.2.12 packages, respectively [26, 10]. The proposed TOD and OI methods, complete analysis scripts, and reproduction instructions are available from the kmaudit project repository at https://github.com/fespuny/kmaudit. The version of kmaudit that includes the reproduction materials corresponding to this article is permanently archived on Zenodo [7].

Data Availability Statement

The analysis data that support the findings of this study are openly available in the versioned kmaudit archive on Zenodo at doi:10.5281/zenodo.24134374 [7]. The archive includes the simulation level results and derived analysis data required to reproduce the reported figures, tables, model fits, and validation results. Benchmark analyses use publicly available datasets which are distributed through the R packages cited in this article and remain subject to their original licences and terms of use.

Appendix A Supplementary Results for Event Ordering

This appendix provides technical results and proofs supporting the event ordering theory developed in Section 3. Throughout, observed failure times are assumed distinct, d⁡(ti)≤1d(t_{i})\leq 1, and all observed event types other than type kk are aggregated into the competing event label EcE_{c}. This aggregation does not affect the arguments, which depend only on whether an observed failure is of type kk or a competing type.

  • •

    Appendix A.1 provides the complete derivation of the Local Empirical Overestimation Inflation Formula in Equation (12).

  • •

    Appendix A.2 discusses intervening censoring structures and derives the closed-form uncensored upper bound for maximal KM overestimation.

A.1 Derivation of the Local Empirical Overestimation Inflation Formula

This appendix derives the exact local increase in empirical cause-specific KM overestimation created by transposing an adjacent pair of failure events: (Ek,Ec)(E_{k},E_{c}) into (Ec,Ek)(E_{c},E_{k}). Consider two consecutive failure times ta<tbt_{a}<t_{b} with no intervening failures and with c≥0c\geq 0 censored observations occurring between them. Let

ra=r⁡(ta−),rb=r⁡(tb−)=ra−1−c.r_{a}=r(t_{a}^{-}),\qquad r_{b}=r(t_{b}^{-})=r_{a}-1-c.

Define

Dprev=1−S^KM,k​(ta−)−F^kA​J​(ta−)D_{\mathrm{prev}}=1-\hat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{a}^{-})-\hat{F}_{k}^{AJ}(t_{a}^{-})

and

S^PL,prev=S^PL​(ta−).\hat{S}_{\mathrm{PL,prev}}=\hat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t_{a}^{-}).

A.1.1 Original Allocation: (Ek,Ec)(E_{k},E_{c})

Under the original sequence (Ek,Ec)(E_{k},E_{c}), the event of type kk occurs at tat_{a}. The KM complement therefore updates as

1−S^KM,k​(tb+)\displaystyle 1-\hat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{b}^{+}) =1−S^KM,k​(ta−)​(1−1ra)\displaystyle=1-\hat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{a}^{-})\left(1-\frac{1}{r_{a}}\right) (26)
=1−S^KM,k​(ta−)+S^KM,k​(ta−)ra.\displaystyle=1-\hat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{a}^{-})+\frac{\hat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{a}^{-})}{r_{a}}. (27)

Similarly, the AJ estimator updates as

F^kA​J​(tb+)=F^kA​J​(ta−)+S^PL,prevra.\hat{F}_{k}^{AJ}(t_{b}^{+})=\hat{F}_{k}^{AJ}(t_{a}^{-})+\frac{\hat{S}_{\mathrm{PL,prev}}}{r_{a}}. (28)

Consequently,

B^k​(tb+)=Dprev+S^KM,k​(ta−)−S^PL,prevra.\hat{B}_{k}(t_{b}^{+})=D_{\mathrm{prev}}+\frac{\hat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{a}^{-})-\hat{S}_{\mathrm{PL,prev}}}{r_{a}}. (29)

A.1.2 Transposed Allocation: (Ec,Ek)(E_{c},E_{k})

Under the transposed sequence (Ec,Ek)(E_{c},E_{k}), the competing event occurs first. The KM complement therefore becomes

1−S^KM,k′​(tb+)\displaystyle 1-\hat{S}^{\prime}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{b}^{+}) =1−S^KM,k​(ta−)​(1−1rb)\displaystyle=1-\hat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{a}^{-})\left(1-\frac{1}{r_{b}}\right) (30)
=1−S^KM,k​(ta−)+S^KM,k​(ta−)rb.\displaystyle=1-\hat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{a}^{-})+\frac{\hat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}(t_{a}^{-})}{r_{b}}. (31)

For the AJ estimator, the competing event first reduces overall product limit survival to

S^PL,prev​(1−1ra).\hat{S}_{\mathrm{PL,prev}}\left(1-\frac{1}{r_{a}}\right).

The subsequent cause-kk event then contributes

S^PL,prev​(ra−1)ra​rb.\frac{\hat{S}_{\mathrm{PL,prev}}(r_{a}-1)}{r_{a}r_{b}}.

Hence

F^kAJ′(tb+)=F^kA​J(ta−)+S^PL,prev​(ra−1)ra​rb.\hat{F}_{k}^{AJ\,\prime}(t_{b}^{+})=\hat{F}_{k}^{AJ}(t_{a}^{-})+\frac{\hat{S}_{\mathrm{PL,prev}}(r_{a}-1)}{r_{a}r_{b}}. (32)

A.1.3 Difference in Empirical Overestimation (Exact Local Inflation Formula)

The change in empirical KM overestimation induced by the transposition is

Δ​B^k​(tb+)=B^k′​(tb+)−B^k​(tb+).\Delta\hat{B}_{k}(t_{b}^{+})=\hat{B}_{k}^{\prime}(t_{b}^{+})-\hat{B}_{k}(t_{b}^{+}).

Substituting the preceding expressions and simplifying yields

Δ​B^k​(tb+)=Dprev​(ra−rb)+S^PL,prevra​rb.\Delta\hat{B}_{k}(t_{b}^{+})=\frac{D_{\mathrm{prev}}(r_{a}-r_{b})+\hat{S}_{\mathrm{PL,prev}}}{r_{a}r_{b}}.

Since

ra−rb=1+c,r_{a}-r_{b}=1+c,

we obtain

Δ​B^k​(tb+)=Dprev​(1+c)+S^PL,prevra​rb\boxed{\Delta\hat{B}_{k}(t_{b}^{+})=\frac{D_{\mathrm{prev}}(1+c)+\hat{S}_{\mathrm{PL,prev}}}{r_{a}r_{b}}} (33)

which is exactly the expression reported in Equation (12). Because

Dprev≥0,S^PL,prev>0,ra​rb>0,D_{\mathrm{prev}}\geq 0,\qquad\hat{S}_{\mathrm{PL,prev}}>0,\qquad r_{a}r_{b}>0,

it follows immediately that

Δ​B^k​(tb+)>0.\Delta\hat{B}_{k}(t_{b}^{+})>0.

Therefore removing an inversion by an adjacent transposition strictly increases empirical cause-specific KM overestimation. ∎

A.2 Extensions and Sharp Upper Bound

Intervening Censoring Structures.

The event ordering results developed in Section 3 extend directly to cohorts subject to intervening right censoring. Let c≥0c\geq 0 denote the number of individuals censored between two adjacent failure events occurring at times ta<tbt_{a}<t_{b}. The Local Empirical Overestimation Inflation Formula in Equation (12) was derived allowing arbitrary values of cc through the relationship rb=ra−1−cr_{b}=r_{a}-1-c, and therefore already incorporates censoring occurring between adjacent failure events. Because Equation (12) remains strictly positive for all admissible values of cc, Δ​B^k​(tb+)>0\Delta\hat{B}_{k}(t_{b}^{+})>0, removing an inversion by an adjacent transposition continues to increase empirical KM overestimation in the presence of right censoring. Consequently, the monotonic inversion reduction argument underlying Theorem 1 remains valid under arbitrary independent right censoring structures.

Closed-Form Evaluation of the Maximal Uncensored Overestimation.

Theorem 1 identifies the event ordering that maximizes cause-specific KM risk at the study horizon and, by Corollary 1, the corresponding theoretical horizon overestimation. Consider an uncensored cohort of size NN containing nkn_{k} events of type kk and ncn_{c} competing events. Because the Aalen–Johansen estimator reduces to the observed event proportion under complete follow-up,

F^kAJ​(tmax)=nkN.\widehat{F}_{k}^{\mathrm{AJ}}(t_{\max})=\frac{n_{k}}{N}.

Under the maximal-overestimation configuration 𝒮F∗=(Ec,…,Ec,Ek,…,Ek)\mathcal{S}_{F}^{\ast}=(E_{c},\ldots,E_{c},E_{k},\ldots,E_{k}), all competing events occur before all events of type kk. The corresponding KM survival estimator therefore satisfies

S^KM,kmax​(tmax)=∏j=0nk−1(1−1N−nc−j)=N−nc−nkN−nc.\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}^{\max}(t_{\max})=\prod_{j=0}^{n_{k}-1}\left(1-\frac{1}{N-n_{c}-j}\right)=\frac{N-n_{c}-n_{k}}{N-n_{c}}.

Taking complements gives

1−S^KM,kmax​(tmax)=nkN−nc.1-\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{KM},k}^{\max}(t_{\max})=\frac{n_{k}}{N-n_{c}}.

Hence the maximal attainable empirical overestimation is

B^kmax​(tmax)=nkN−nc−nkN=nk​ncN⁡(N−nc).\widehat{B}_{k}^{\max}(t_{\max})=\frac{n_{k}}{N-n_{c}}-\frac{n_{k}}{N}=\frac{n_{k}n_{c}}{N(N-n_{c})}. (34)

Equation (34) provides a sharp closed-form upper bound for empirical KM overestimation under complete follow-up. The bound depends only on the numbers of events of interest and competing events, and is attained precisely under the zero inversion ordering characterized by Theorem 1.

Appendix B Simulation Studies

This appendix mainly provides supplementary details for the simulation studies reported in Section 6.

  • •

    Appendix B.1 describes the frequency-ordering simulation design and benchmarking;

  • •

    Appendix B.2 reports calibration and quality control results;

  • •

    Appendix B.3 provides supplementary results for the censoring stress test;
