    Appendix B.4 provides numerical validation of the Product Limit Error Equivalence.

B.1 Frequency & OI Space Simulation Design and Benchmarking

The simulation experiments reported in Sections 6.3 and 7 were generated using a Frequency-OI space simulation design rather than a conventional parameter space factorial design. The design was developed in three stages.

First, a calibration phase was performed using a large collection of latent competing risks processes. For each combination of latent Weibull parameters, the generated competing event frequency and Order Index (OI) were recorded. This produced an empirical calibration cloud linking latent parameter configurations to simulated observable quantities.

Second, the frequency & ordering space generated by the calibration cloud was evaluated. Preliminary experiments showed that direct parameter space sampling produced highly uneven coverage of the frequency & OI space, with some combinations of competing event frequency and event ordering markedly overrepresented and others sparsely represented.

Third, an occupancy aware sampling procedure was developed to improve coverage of the simulated space. Calibration points were sampled from the empirical calibration cloud using inverse occupancy weighting, thereby increasing the representation of sparsely populated regions while preserving the diversity of calibration configurations. The weighting scheme was tuned using the occupancy diagnostics reported in Appendix B.2.

Using this approach, simulated datasets were generated with target sample size N=500N=500 and approximately 20% independent right censoring. A total of Nt​o​t​a​l=100×800=80,000N_{total}=100\times 800=80,000 datasets were produced. The resulting simulation design achieved broad coverage of the frequency & ordering space and allowed empirical investigation of KM overestimation beyond the limited set of ordering settings considered in earlier experiments. For each simulated dataset, the following quantities were recorded:

  • •

    censoring proportion,

  • •

    competing event frequency,

  • •

    Order Index,

  • •

    KM risks,

  • •

    cumulative incidence functions,

  • •

    empirical cause-specific KM overestimation,

  • •

    empirical total KM overestimation (TOD).

Model benchmarking and sensitivity analysis.

The resulting datasets were used to evaluate how frequency, ordering, TOD, and censoring jointly influence competing risks overestimation (Table 2). Table B1 reports the complete model search considered during development of the practical interpretation framework presented in Section 7. Although the three-factor interaction model achieved the highest simulation adjusted R2R^{2}, the TOD×\timesOI model yielded the strongest benchmark validation performance (MAE=0.007) and therefore formed the basis of the developed interpretation framework.

As a sensitivity analysis, all models were re-fitted using occupancy balanced undersampling, with 250 simulated datasets drawn for each Frequency by OI cell in a 10 ×\times 10 discretisation grid. The resulting model coefficient, adjusted R2R^{2} and benchmark validation values were nearly identical to those obtained under the original design. In particular, the TOD and TOD ×\times OI models retained both their coefficient structure and relative performance, suggesting that the proposed interpretation framework is not sensitive to the occupancy structure of the simulated space.

To examine practical predictive performance in detail, the strongest benchmark performing models were applied directly to the six benchmark datasets. Table B2 compares observed and predicted cause-specific overestimation. The principal validation results are summarised in the main text Table 2.

B.2 Calibration and Coverage Assessment

The simulation design was evaluated using calibration and occupancy diagnostics. Calibration quality was assessed by comparing simulation generated quantities with their corresponding calibration targets.

Across the complete simulation design, the mean absolute frequency calibration error was approximately 0.016, while the mean absolute Order Index calibration error was approximately 0.025. These values indicate that the calibration procedure successfully generated datasets spanning the intended regions of the frequency–ordering space.

Coverage of the calibration target space was assessed using a 20×2020\times 20 occupancy grid defined by observed competing event frequency and observed Order Index. Every occupancy cell contained simulated datasets, indicating complete space coverage without occupancy voids (at 0.05 resolution). The median occupancy exceeded 3,800 datasets per cell and the occupancy coefficient of variation was approximately 0.15, representing a clear improvement over earlier simulation designs. To avoid excessive concentration of simulations within a small subset of calibration points, several diagnostics of calibration cloud diversity were examined. These included the effective sample size, the distribution of calibration point usage, and the coefficient of variation of calibration point frequencies. The adopted occupancy aware weighting scheme maintained high calibration diversity while improving realised space coverage.

The simulation design achieved three objectives simultaneously:

  1. 1.

    accurate calibration of competing event frequency;

  2. 2.

    accurate calibration of event ordering;

  3. 3.

    broad and approximately uniform coverage of the joint frequency & ordering space.

Consequently, the simulation study provides a broad and balanced coverage of the frequency-ordering space.

B.3 Additional Results for the Censoring Stress Test

This section provides detailed numerical summaries for the censoring settings investigated in Section 6.4. Table B3 contains both measures of total overestimation and the diagnostic quantities used in the numerical validation reported subsequently in Appendix B.4. Observed censoring frequencies closely matched their intended targets throughout the simulation study. Detailed calibration summaries for resulting censoring levels and mean follow-up times are available from the simulation quality control outputs. Increasing censoring substantially reduced observed follow-up time and increased variability, while having little effect on the underlying total overestimation signal.

Table B3 provides detailed Monte Carlo summaries for the five censoring settings investigated in Section 6.4. The most important observation is the stability of mean total overestimation across censoring settings. At five years, mean total overestimation ranged only from approximately 0.207 in the uncensored setting to approximately 0.209 under the heaviest censoring setting. In contrast, variability increased markedly as censoring intensified. The standard deviation of total overestimation at five years increased from approximately 0.027 in the uncensored setting to approximately 0.121 under heavy censoring, corresponding to an approximately 4.5-fold increase in variability.

B.4 Finite Sample Validation of Product Limit Error Equivalence

The Product Limit Error Equivalence theorem (Theorem 4) is an exact algebraic identity. The purpose of the simulations reported here is therefore not proof, but numerical confirmation of the finite sample behaviour implied by the theorem.

We evaluated the following prediction implied by the Product Limit Error Equivalence theorem: that the entire finite sample error structure of total overestimation estimation should mirror that of ordinary product limit survival estimation. Figure B1 compares the standard deviation of the total overestimation estimation error,

B^total​(t)−Btotal​(t),\widehat{B}_{\mathrm{total}}(t)-B_{\mathrm{total}}(t),

with the standard deviation of the corresponding product limit survival estimation error,

S^PL​(t)−S​(t).\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t)-S(t).

Across all censoring settings and evaluation times, the standard deviations of the two error processes were numerically indistinguishable, with the maximum observed difference equal to 3.12×10−173.12\times 10^{-17}. Furthermore, the identity residual

Δ⁡(t)=[B^total​(t)−Btotal​(t)]−[S^PL​(t)−S⁡(t)]\Delta(t)=\Big[\widehat{B}_{\mathrm{total}}(t)-B_{\mathrm{total}}(t)\Big]-\Big[\widehat{S}_{\mathrm{PL}}(t)-S(t)\Big]

remained at machine precision throughout the study. The maximum absolute residual observed across all simulation runs was 2.22×10−162.22\times 10^{-16}, while the empirical correlation between the two error processes remained above 0.99999999999999980.9999999999999998.

Figures 4 and B1 demonstrate that censoring primarily reduces precision rather than altering the magnitude of competing risks overestimation, and that inference for total overestimation behaves in finite samples exactly as predicted by the Product Limit Error Equivalence theorem.
